description: We are a group of students who want to share our skills, ideas, and creativity through this hackathon. We see this event as a chance to try something new, work together, and show what we can do. We also want to gain experience, learn new things, and improve our skills as a team.
summary: FIRE MEMORY is a Philippine satellite fire-monitoring dashboard powered by interactive mapping, data visualization, and Google Gemini. Standard hotspot maps lack historical context, while legacy MODIS and newer VIIRS NASA sensors detect heat differently, obscuring true seasonal trends. FIRE MEMORY unifies both satellite records onto a consistent scale, distinguishes missing coverage from inactivity, and evaluates each period against typical same-season history. Through interactive maps, historical calendars, priority watchlists, exportable reports, and a verified Advisory AI, local disaster management offices can separate genuine seasonal surges from sensor shifts and coordinate responsible field verification.
details:
What exactly does it do? FIRE MEMORY is a Philippine satellite fire-monitoring dashboard that puts heat detections into clear historical context. Users can explore an interactive map across provinces or custom drawn areas, inspect a multi-year monthly calendar that separates missing coverage from inactivity, see whether a month is below, near, above, or unusually high compared with the same month in past years, generate grounded verification advisories for local disaster teams, and download spreadsheet reports.

How does it work? The system takes NASA MODIS and VIIRS thermal detection records, matches them to Philippine provinces and local grid areas by month, and calibrates older MODIS counts onto a comparable VIIRS-equivalent scale using overlapping years while openly displaying accuracy and error metrics. A cloud database stores regional history alongside live satellite feeds, and the built-in AI reads only those verified statistics to provide safe, non-predictive monitoring guidance without inventing numbers or claiming unverified fires.

What benefits does it have?

  • Prevents sensor transitions between older MODIS and newer VIIRS satellites from looking like sudden changes in fire activity.
  • Evaluates every period against the same calendar month in prior years for fair seasonal comparisons.
  • Keeps missing satellite coverage clearly marked rather than treating absent data as zero.
  • Helps local disaster management offices and fire verification teams spot genuine surges faster with transparent data and downloadable reports.

What do you hope to achieve? Our immediate goal is to give Philippine local disaster offices, responders, and researchers a reliable monitoring aid to detect unusual seasonal activity and coordinate timely ground verification. Long term, we hope to incorporate earlier multi-decade satellite archives, validate regional calibration factors with emergency agencies, and scale the platform to cover additional municipalities and global regions.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, SQL, HTML, CSS, and SVG
  • Frameworks and Libraries: Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Leaflet MarkerCluster, Turf.js, Recharts, Zod, PapaParse, and jsPDF
  • Backend, AI, and Hosting: Supabase (PostgreSQL), Google Gemini API, Node.js, Git, GitHub, and Vercel
  • Geospatial Data and Basemaps: NASA LANCE FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS), geoBoundaries, OpenStreetMap, CARTO, and Esri
  • Software and Hardware: ESLint, standard development laptops, and modern web browsers (no custom hardware sensors used)
